phonemes.desc: Wh is pronounced f (older dialects a breathy wh); the stressed first syllable.
Rolled r followed by a short open o.

pronunciation.approximation: 'FEE-roh' — the wh is an f-sound in most modern Māori, and the r is trilled.

kin.label: Full form
kin.form: Whiro-te-tipua, 'Whiro the goblin/supernatural being' (Grey, Polynesian Mythology)

kin.label: Comparative
kin.form: Hiro, a Tahitian atua of the underworld — a plausible eastern cognate (Tregear, Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary; treated cautiously by Craig)

kin.label: His antagonist
kin.form: Tāne-mahuta, lord of forests and light — the paired opposite in the surviving myths

pronunciation.note: Whiro is single-tier Tier 2: ASCII preserves everything the Māori name requires; the digraph wh already encodes the f-sound to those who know Māori orthography. His epithet -te-tipua marks him as a tipua, a goblin-like being — a class, not a compliment.

domains.title: Whiro
domains.subtitle: Darkness
domains.lead: Whiro is the Māori personification of darkness, evil, and death — the adversary of Tāne and the lord of the night-world. He sends sickness, commands the reptiles of the night, and, in the oldest accounts, wars against every ascent toward light, knowledge, and life.

cards.name: Lord of Darkness
cards.desc: He rules the Pō, the realm of night and the dead that lies beneath and behind the world of light.

cards.name: Enemy of Tāne
cards.desc: He battles Tāne at every ascent — the cosmic rival who must be defeated for knowledge to come down.

cards.name: Sender of Sickness
cards.desc: Disease is his assault; the tohunga's art was, in origin, the war against his influences.

cards.name: Father of the Lizards
cards.desc: He is styled ancestor of the ngarara, the reptiles — the creatures Māori tradition reads as his embodied kin.

symbols.name: The Lizard (Moko/Ngarara)
symbols.meaning: His embodied kin — reptiles were feared as carriers of his malign influence (hence 'the lizard of death')

symbols.name: The Night (Pō)
symbols.meaning: His domain — the darkness that preceded light and that receives the dead

symbols.name: The War-Party of Spirits
symbols.meaning: The host of atua he leads against the worlds of light, named in accounts of Tāne's battles

symbols.name: Sickness (Mate)
symbols.meaning: The weapon he hurls — illness conceived as an invading atua to be fought and expelled

symbols.name: The Underworld Path
symbols.meaning: The descent to Rarohenga over which, in some traditions, he holds final power

mythology.lead: Whiro's mythology is an antagonist's dossier — he exists in the Māori corpus chiefly as the power Tāne and the tohunga must overcome. The sources are nineteenth-century records of oral tradition (Grey 1855; White 1887–90; Best 1925), and they agree on his office while differing on his genealogy and extent.

myths.title: The War Over the Baskets of Knowledge
myths.text: In the great myth preserved by George Grey (Polynesian Mythology, 1855; Nga Mahi a nga Tupuna), Tāne ascends through the layered heavens to obtain the three baskets of knowledge (ngā kete o te wānanga) for humankind. Whiro — Whiro-te-tipua — marshals the powers of darkness against the ascent, and the myth is explicitly a war: each heaven is contested, and Tāne prevails only with the aid of the winds and ancestor-gods above. Grey's text, dictated by Māori experts in the 1850s, is our fullest witness; the Tūhoe versions add that the battle-lines were drawn anew in each heaven as Tāne climbed. The variant accounts collected by Elsdon BestThe variant accounts collected by Elsdon Best (Tūhoe, 1925) and John White (Ancient History of the Maori) fill in different battle-lines. Whatever the version, the structure is fixed: knowledge descends only through victory over darkness, and darkness is a person who resents the delivery.

myths.title: Whiro and the Descent to Pō
myths.text: Māori eschatology sends the dead (ngā mate) to the underworld of Rarohenga, in the keeping of the goddess Hine-nui-te-pō. Within that realm the sources assign Whiro a dreadful office: Best (Tūhoe, 1925) records that Whiro consumes the dead — the final extinction that awaits those who pass fully into his night — while other authorities make the underworld a guarded, not devoured, existence. Best records how carefully the dying were guarded: kin kept vigil so the soul's journey began rightly, for a misstep on the path meant falling among the powers that answered to Whiro rather than to the ancestors. The disagreement is itself instructive:The disagreement is itself instructive: Māori tradition was not systematic about its dark gods. What holds across the accounts is the direction of dread: after death lies a jurisdiction Whiro administers, and his administration is nothing to hope for.

myths.title: The Ngarara His Children
myths.text: Whiro's epithet 'the lizard of death' is not metaphor alone: Māori genealogical chant makes him ancestor of the ngarara — the lizards, tuatara, and reptiles — whose cold eye and sudden movement marked them as his embodied kin (Best, Tūhoe; Orbell, A Concise Encyclopedia of Māori Myth and Legend, 1998). A lizard in the house could be an omen or an emissary; killing one carelessly was dangerous. The tuatara — a living fossil, stranger than any creature the Māori had names for — was the most charged of all his children, and some traditions set it as guardian at the very threshold of Hine-nui-te-pō. The genealogy does ecological work:The genealogy does ecological work: it assigns the island's most alien-seeming creatures to the one god who is himself alien to the world of light. The reptiles are Whiro's diaspora — small darknesses walking in the daylight world.

myths.title: Illness as His Assault
myths.text: In Māori medical tradition, sickness (mate) was the work of hostile atua, and Whiro stood behind the host: Best's ethnography (Tūhoe; 'Maori Medical Lore') describes the tohunga diagnosing which atua had 'shot' the patient and performing rites to drive the invader out. The rite was theater as much as medicine: the tohunga named the invading atua aloud, drove it toward the sea with the village's shouting, and bound the patient with cords — law, drama, and therapy in one operation. The afflictions attributed to Whiro's sideThe afflictions attributed to Whiro's side of the spirit world were grave and creeping — the wasting illnesses, the illnesses that came at night. The practical corollary was a therapy of confrontation: healing was a battle with Whiro's agents, fought with chant, gesture, and the authority of ancestors who had beaten him before. Illness had an enemy, and therefore a remedy.

lore.syncretism: The missionaries who translated Māori cosmology reached immediately for their own devil — and George Grey's English Polynesian Mythology (1855) already frames Whiro as a 'personification of evil' in Victorian moral vocabulary, a reading modern scholarship (Orbell; Craig) treats as an over-Christianization of a more ambivalent figure. Whiro is darkness and death, but Māori tradition also treats night as generative — the Pō is where spirits dwell and from which thought ascends — so his 'evil' is an office in a balanced cosmos, not a fallen angel's rebellion. In the modern renaissance, Whiro has been reclaimed as exactly that: a necessary power, appearing as an antagonist in Māori-language fiction, film, and graphic narrative where a culture works out its relationship to sickness, night, and fear on its own terms rather than Christianity's.
lore.culturalLegacy: Whiro was never worshiped — he had no marae, no priesthood, no offering; his 'cult' is a vocabulary of avoidance and exorcism. His legacy runs through language and practice instead: the fear of lizards as omens, the ritual cautions of the night, and the entire therapeutic tradition of the tohunga, whose first question — which atua did this? — assumes his world. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries Whiro has become a figure of the Māori cultural renaissance: a dignified, fully Māori face for the dark side of existence, used in health frameworks that treat illness within a Māori cosmology (te ao Māori models of wellbeing explicitly name and counter the atua of affliction). A god nobody prayed to thus shapes how a people still prays for health — his lasting temple is the rite that casts him out.
lore.extendedMeditation: Whiro is a lesson in how a culture personifies what it fears without worshiping it. The Greeks had Éris; the Māori have Whiro — a being defined entirely by opposition, known through the myths of his defeats. Yet the Māori construction is subtler than a devil: Whiro is not fallen but resident — darkness is part of the building, the Pō beneath the Ao, and a cosmos without him would be a day without night, unthinkable and infertile. His myths are therefore really about the other side: Tāne's knowledge matters because Whiro contested it; the tohunga's cure works because Whiro sent the sickness. To study Whiro is to study a people's map of dread — lizards, wasting illness, the path of the dead — drawn with such precision that the map became the means of rescue. Fear, given a genealogy, can be argued with.
lore.archaeology: As with most Māori atua, there is no material representation of Whiro: Māori religion was aniconic, and no carving, amulet, or structure is identified with him — the dread of his likeness would itself have been a contradiction. The relevant archaeology is contextual: the carved meeting houses whose pou (posts) embody ancestors of light, set against the prohibitions and ritual zones around burial caves and urupā, where his jurisdiction was strongest. Traditional Māori rock art and tattoo (tā moko) employ curvilinear forms sometimes read as reptilian, but attributing them to Whiro exceeds the evidence. The 'sites' of Whiro are instead the documented places of night practice — the sickbed, the burial ground, the lizard-haunted gully — mapped for us by Best's ethnography rather than by excavation.
